title: Two philosophies, and what actually survived
objective: By the end of this lesson you can state what each approach optimised for, explain why the distinction matters less than it once did, and say which of its consequences you can still observe today.

blocks.text: For a long time the field had two answers to one question: should an instruction set be large and expressive, or small and regular? Both approaches were reasonable given the constraints of their time, and the interesting part is not who won but which constraints changed.

The complex approach was right when memory was scarce and expensive and much code was written by hand: an instruction that did more meant a smaller program and less typing. The reduced approach became right when compilers improved and memory became cheap: what mattered then was hardware that could be made fast, and regular instructions are far easier to pipeline.

blocks.title: The decisive argument was about pipelines, which is the next module
blocks.text: Fixed-length, regular instructions can be decoded before you know what they are, which is what makes it practical to have several in flight at once. Variable-length instructions must be partly decoded to find where the next one begins. That single property is most of why the reduced approach won the architectural argument — and understanding why is the reason the pipeline module comes shortly after this one.

Neither side won cleanly. Modern x86-64 processors decode their complex instructions into simpler internal operations and then execute those with the same techniques a reduced design uses. The external contract stayed complex, for compatibility; the internal implementation became something else entirely. That is the ISA-versus-implementation split from the previous lesson, at its largest scale.

items: The instruction set you program against is a compatibility surface, not a description of the hardware
A complex instruction may become several internal operations, or occasionally one
Reduced designs also grew: modern aarch64 and RISC-V have far more instructions than the original arguments imagined
The practical difference today is decoding cost, code density, and how easy the ISA is to implement — not a philosophy

rows: Fixed 4 bytes (RISC-V also has a 2-byte compressed form)
Instructions that read and write memory

blocks.title: Variable length is why a corrupted address produces nonsense
blocks.text: On x86-64, starting to disassemble one byte late produces a completely different, still-valid-looking instruction stream, because the decoder simply reads whatever is there. On a fixed-length architecture that cannot happen — every instruction starts on a four-byte boundary. This is a real consideration when reading disassembly, and it is one of the reasons the Assembly course spends time on where instruction boundaries actually are.

blocks.caption: Measured: real aarch64 object code, addresses and bytes
lines: # Every address advances by exactly 4, and every instruction is 4 bytes.
# Note also the load-store rule in action: two ldr instructions bring the
# values in, and the add works only on registers.

blocks.text: A four-byte instruction cannot contain a 64-bit constant, so large values must be assembled from several instructions. This is the price paid for the regularity, and it is directly visible in generated code.

blocks.caption: Measured: building one 64-bit constant on aarch64
lines: movk  x8, #0x71fb, lsl #16        <- three instructions to place
movk  w9, #0x3ade, lsl #16        <- two more for the 32-bit one
# A variable-length architecture would encode the constant inline in one
# instruction. That is the density advantage — paid for with a decoder
# that must read an instruction to learn where it ends.

blocks.text: The load-store rule is the one that shapes code

The rule that only load and store touch memory has more effect on generated code than any other difference. It means every computation happens between registers, and any value from memory must be loaded first and stored back explicitly. That makes the cost of memory access visible in the instruction stream, which the next module builds on directly.

blocks.title: Compare the two on your own machine
steps: Write a small C function that adds two array elements and stores the result
Compile with: cc -S -O2 f.c -o -    and read the assembly for your architecture
Count how many instructions touch memory and how many operate only on registers
If you have a cross-compiler or an online compiler, produce the same function for the other architecture and compare
Compile a whole small program and compare the size of the machine code section: size ./prog
Run: objdump -d ./prog | head -30    and look at the byte counts per instruction
On x86-64, note that the byte counts vary; on aarch64, note that they do not
Explain in one sentence why that difference matters for a pipeline
blocks.expected: Two instruction streams for the same function, a count of memory-touching instructions, and a direct observation of fixed versus variable length in the byte columns. That last observation is the one the pipeline module will assume you have made.

cheatsheet: Complex sets: many instructions, variable length, many can touch memory
Reduced sets: few regular instructions, fixed length, only load and store touch memory
Complex suited scarce memory and hand-written assembly; reduced suited compilers and fast hardware
Fixed-length, regular instructions are far easier to pipeline — that was the decisive argument
Modern x86-64 decodes complex instructions into simpler internal operations
The ISA is a compatibility surface, not a description of the hardware
x86-64 instructions are 1 to 15 bytes; aarch64 is fixed at 4
Variable length means disassembling from the wrong offset yields plausible nonsense
The load-store rule makes the cost of memory access visible in the instruction stream

checkpoint.prompt: Why are fixed-length instructions easier to pipeline?

choices.B: The next instruction's position is known without decoding this one, so several can be fetched and decoded at once

checkpoint.explanation: With variable length you must partly decode an instruction to learn where the next begins. That serialisation is what makes overlapping harder, and it was the decisive argument in the debate.

checkpoint.prompt: A modern x86-64 processor executes complex instructions. How?

choices.A: Directly, in dedicated hardware per instruction
choices.B: It decodes them into simpler internal operations and executes those with the same techniques a reduced design uses

checkpoint.explanation: The external contract stayed complex for compatibility while the implementation became something else. That is the ISA-versus-implementation split at its largest scale.

checkpoint.prompt: You disassemble x86-64 code starting one byte too late. What do you see?

choices.B: A completely different but still plausible-looking instruction stream, because the decoder reads whatever bytes are there

checkpoint.explanation: Variable-length encoding has no alignment to resynchronise on. A fixed-length architecture cannot have this problem, since every instruction begins on a four-byte boundary.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the load-store rule change about generated code?

choices.B: Every computation happens between registers, so memory access appears explicitly as separate load and store instructions
choices.C: It removes the need for a cache

checkpoint.explanation: The cost of touching memory becomes visible in the instruction stream rather than hidden inside an arithmetic instruction, which is what the following modules build their reasoning on.
